items.prompt: What is a prototype?
choices: A cheap stand-in used to get a reaction early
The finished product shipped to every customer
A written list of every line of code to write
A bug report filed after the launch date
items.explanation: A prototype is a cheap stand-in used to get a reaction before committing to the real build.

items.prompt: What does fidelity mean for a prototype?
choices: How many people took part in the final test
How closely it resembles the finished product
How long the team spent arguing about the design
How much the team likes the final design
items.explanation: Fidelity is resemblance to the finished product in look, behavior and speed.

items.prompt: Which rung is the cheapest to build?
choices: Wireframe
Clickable prototype
Coded prototype
Paper sketch
items.explanation: A paper sketch takes about 3 hours in this unit's numbers.

items.prompt: Which rung takes the most hours to build?
choices: Coded prototype
Paper sketch
Wireframe
Clickable prototype
items.explanation: The coded prototype is about 90 hours, the most of the four rungs.

items.prompt: Which rung is made of linked screens you can tap through?
choices: Wireframe
Paper sketch
Clickable prototype
Coded prototype
items.explanation: A clickable prototype links static screens so a person can tap through the flow.

items.prompt: Can a prototype look polished and still behave nothing like the real thing?
choices: No, polish always means the behavior is realistic
No, because prototypes cannot ever look polished
Yes, but only when the prototype was fully coded
Yes, since look and behavior are separate things
items.explanation: Fidelity is not one dial. A static mockup can look perfect while nothing responds.

items.prompt: About how many hours does a paper sketch take in this unit?
choices: 10 hours
3 hours
28 hours
90 hours
items.explanation: Paper sketch 3, wireframe 10, clickable 28, coded 90.

items.prompt: Why test with a stand-in before building the real thing?
choices: Real builds are never allowed before a test
Stand-ins are always more accurate than real builds
A wrong idea is still cheap to catch at that point
Designers are not able to read the real code
items.explanation: The earlier a wrong idea is caught, the less has been spent on it.

items.prompt: A mockup looks identical to the finished app, but none of its buttons respond. How is its fidelity best described?
choices: High in both look and behavior, since it appears finished
High in look, low in behavior
Low in both look and behavior, since nothing responds
Low in look but high in behavior, since it is inert
items.explanation: Look and behavior are separate. This mockup matches the finished look but fakes all behavior.
items.reference:
The fidelity spectrum
paper sketch: 3 hrs, tests overall order
wireframe: 10 hrs, tests layout and wording
clickable: 28 hrs, tests the flow end to end
coded: 90 hrs, tests real feel and data
Why: each rung answers something the one below cannot, at a higher cost.
items.learnMore:
Fidelity is not one dial

A prototype can look finished while behaving nothing like the real thing, or look rough while behaving exactly like it. Pick the rung by what the question needs, not by how polished the result looks.

Common mistake

Equating a polished look with realistic behavior. A static mockup can be perfect visually and still say nothing about the flow.
items.reflection: Think of a time you checked an idea cheaply before committing to it, such as a rough plan before a big purchase. What was your paper sketch?

items.prompt: What is the cheapest rung that can test whether the order of the steps in a flow makes sense?
choices: A coded prototype wired to the live checkout
A single static wireframe of the last screen
A paper sketch flipped by hand in order
A load test run with simulated live traffic
items.explanation: Order is a structural question and a paper sketch can answer it for about 3 hours of work.

items.prompt: How many 7-day loops fit in a 28-day window?
items.explanation: 28 divided by 7 is 4.

items.prompt: How many 14-day loops fit in a 28-day window?
items.explanation: 28 divided by 14 is 2.

items.prompt: How many 1-day loops fit in a 28-day window?
items.explanation: 28 divided by 1 is 28.

items.prompt: What is a feedback loop?
choices: Build once, ship it, and wait for complaints
Write a long plan, then ask for sign-off
Test the idea only after launching to everyone
Build, show it, learn from it, decide next
items.explanation: A loop is the repeating cycle of build, show, learn and decide.

items.prompt: What does a shorter loop give you in a fixed window?
choices: Fewer people to test with
A higher cost for each separate test
More chances to catch a wrong idea
A longer wait before the first answer
items.explanation: More loops fit, so more mistakes can be caught and fixed in time.

items.prompt: When does the loop stop feeding itself?
choices: When the first person we show it to says they like it
When the design tool has run out of screens to show
When everyone on the team happens to agree with it
When the answer justifies the next step or shipping
items.explanation: The loop continues until confidence matches the cost of being wrong.

items.prompt: How many 21-day loops fit in a 28-day window?
items.explanation: 28 divided by 21 is 1.33, rounded down to 1.

items.prompt: What does the learn step of a loop produce?
choices: A finished product ready to ship
A new fidelity level for the next step
A result: confirmed, wrong, or unclear
A signed approval from the whole team
items.explanation: After showing the prototype, you learn whether the idea held, failed, or needs more clarity.

items.prompt: A team has a 28-day window and each loop takes 9 days. How many full loops fit?
choices: 3, since 28 / 9 is about 3.1 and you round down
4, since 28 / 9 is about 3.1 and you round up
3, since 9 times 3 equals 28 with nothing left over
2, because the final loop needs a spare buffer of days
items.explanation: Only whole loops count, so 3.1 becomes 3.
items.reference:
Loops that fit in 28 days
1 day per loop: 28 tries
3 days: 9 tries
7 days: 4 tries
14 days: 2 tries, 21 days: 1 try
Why: loops = the window divided by the loop length, rounded down, with a floor of one.
items.learnMore:
Loop length is what you buy

Build hours matter because they set the loop length. A shorter loop gives more chances to be wrong and still recover inside a fixed window. The count steps down in whole numbers, so small cuts help most just before a step boundary.

Common mistake

Looking at build cost alone. A 21-day and a 28-day loop both leave one try in a 28-day window, so finishing slightly early buys nothing.
items.reflection: Think of a deadline you have faced. How many real tries did you have before it, and what would a shorter try have bought you?

items.prompt: Loops of 21 days and 28 days both give 1 try in a 28-day window. What is the practical lesson?
choices: The 21-day loop is secretly twice as good as the 28-day loop
The single loop's lesson arrives too late to be acted on
Loop length stops mattering once it passes the 14-day mark
The leftover days allow a second test of the same idea
items.explanation: With only one loop, whatever it teaches has no time left to be acted on.

Whether the prototype has a polished enough look for users

items.prompt: In this unit's numbers, how many hours does a clickable prototype take?
choices: 10 hours
3 hours
90 hours
28 hours
items.explanation: Clickable is 28 hours.

items.prompt: What is the signal quality of a paper sketch here?
items.explanation: Paper sketch signal quality is 30%.

items.prompt: What is the signal quality of a coded prototype here?
items.explanation: Coded signal quality is 95%.

items.prompt: Which step up buys the most extra points per extra hour?
choices: Wireframe to clickable
Clickable to coded
All steps buy the same
Paper to wireframe
items.explanation: Paper to wireframe gives 25 points for 7 hours, 3.57 per hour.

items.prompt: Is a coded prototype three times more trustworthy than a clickable one?
choices: Yes, since it costs about three times as many hours
No, 95% against 75% is far less than three times
Yes, because build hours directly measure trust
No, because coded prototypes carry no signal
items.explanation: It costs 3.21 times the hours but is only 20 points higher.

items.prompt: What does signal quality mean in this unit?
choices: How loudly the test users react to it
How polished the screens happen to look
How well the result predicts behavior
How many users took part in the test
items.explanation: Signal quality is how much you can trust the result as a predictor.

items.prompt: How many hours does a wireframe take here?
choices: 10 hours
3 hours
28 hours
90 hours
items.explanation: Wireframe is 10 hours.

items.prompt: How many extra signal points does clickable to coded add?
choices: 25 points
20 points
62 points
95 points
items.explanation: 95 minus 75 is 20.

items.prompt: Going from clickable (28 hrs, 75%) to coded (90 hrs, 95%) adds how much?
choices: 62 extra hours for 20 extra points
90 extra hours for 20 extra points
62 extra hours for 95 extra points
18 extra hours for 20 extra points
items.explanation: 90 minus 28 is 62 hours and 95 minus 75 is 20 points.
items.reference:
Hours against trust
paper: 3 hrs, signal 30%
wireframe: 10 hrs, signal 55%
clickable: 28 hrs, signal 75%
coded: 90 hrs, signal 95%
Why: the last step costs 62 more hours for 20 more points; the first costs 7 hours for 25.
items.learnMore:
Cost rises faster than trust

Extra points of signal per extra hour fall from 3.57 to 1.11 to 0.32 across the three steps up. Most achievable confidence is available several rungs down.

Common mistake

Assuming three times the hours means three times the trust. Coded costs 3.21 times clickable (90 / 28) but gains only 20 points over 75%.
items.reflection: Think of a purchase where paying much more bought only a little more quality. Where did the curve flatten for you?

Every step up the spectrum adds exactly the same number of signal points
items.explanation: Points per added hour fall sharply at each step, which is the shape of diminishing returns.

items.prompt: Whether the order of steps makes sense is which kind of question?
choices: Interaction feel
Performance
Structural
Pricing
items.explanation: Order and flow are structural.

items.prompt: Whether a swipe feels natural is which kind of question?
choices: Structural
Performance
Wording
Interaction feel
items.explanation: Feel depends on real motion.

items.prompt: Whether a page stays usable with real data volumes is which kind?
choices: Structural
Performance and scale
Interaction feel
Wording
items.explanation: Data volume and latency are performance questions.

items.prompt: Which question can a paper sketch answer?
choices: Does the swipe feel smooth enough?
Does the page stay fast with a million rows?
Is the overall order of the steps right?
Does the drop animation overshoot its target?
items.explanation: A sketch shows structure, not feel or speed.

items.prompt: What does a click-through prototype fake?
choices: The motion between screens but not the destinations
The destinations but not the motion between them
The text on each screen but not how it is laid out
The order of the steps but not the wording used
items.explanation: It can show where you land but not how you get there.

items.prompt: Which rung is enough to test the wording of a button label?
choices: A coded prototype with live data
A load test with simulated traffic
A wireframe
A live experiment with real traffic
items.explanation: Wording is structural, and a wireframe shows wording.

items.prompt: What is the mistake in matching fidelity to a question?
choices: Using a level that cannot answer the question
Using any level below the coded prototype
Using a level that a designer happens to like
Using paper sketches on every kind of project
items.explanation: Fidelity has to be matched to the type of question in both directions.

items.prompt: What does testing a structural question with coded prototype waste?
choices: Hours a load test would have saved later
Weeks confirming what a sketch shows in an hour
Nothing, since higher fidelity is always better
The only chance to test the live performance
items.explanation: Structural questions do not need the expensive rung.

items.prompt: A team tests a swipe-to-delete gesture with linked static screens, and users call it great. What is wrong?
choices: It is a structural question, so the users were asked too late
It is a performance question, so many more users are required
Nothing is wrong, since users approved of the screens
It is a feel question, and static links cannot fake motion
items.explanation: Swipe feel needs real running motion, which a click-through cannot provide.
items.reference:
Match the rung to the question
structural (order, wording): sketch or clickable
interaction feel (drag, swipe): real running interaction
performance and scale: a near-real build
Why: a click-through fakes destinations, not motion, and cannot fake real latency or data.
items.learnMore:
Three kinds of question

Structural questions depend on order and wording. Feel questions depend on real motion and timing. Performance questions depend on real data and network. Each needs a minimum fidelity.

Common mistake

Treating fidelity as high or low in the abstract. The mistake is using a level that cannot answer the question, in either direction.
items.reflection: Think of a decision you tested the wrong way, such as judging a recipe by its photo. What kind of question was it really?

items.prompt: Which question genuinely requires a near-real build?

Is the 'Save for later' link placed where shoppers will look for it?
Does the checkout order make sense to someone seeing it for the first time?
Is the wording of the error message clear to people reading it?
items.explanation: Large data volume and a slow network are performance conditions that cannot be faked.

items.reference:
Coded-first against clickable-first
coded-first: ~4 weeks to first answer, 1 loop in 28 days
clickable-first: ~5 days to first answer, 5 loops
same finding: the flow is confusing

Why: the same structural answer arrived at a fraction of the time and cost.
items.learnMore:
A slow loop has no recovery time

When the first answer arrives at the end of the window, a wrong result leaves no time to fix it. The cheap loop reaches the same finding early enough to redesign and retest.

Common mistake

Defending the build because it taught something. Almost any build teaches something; the question is whether a cheaper one taught the same.

items.prompt: What is the minimum change that would have caught the drag problem?

Build the full live-wired feature before running any test at all
Prototype the real drag gesture with real timing, no backend
Add color and polish to the click-through screens we already have
items.explanation: Raise fidelity only on the axis the question depends on, which is real interaction.

A test that could not fail the real way
